orig_ref: US_24_-_Env_Science_W.pdf, p45-46, FRQ1 (stream dissolved oxygen zones)
descriptor: Stream zones with dissolved oxygen and BOD curves; read diagram, identify variables and control in a macroinvertebrate richness study, explain winter effect, sewage and POP effects.
solution:
(a) Zone C has the lowest dissolved oxygen. *(1 pt)*
(b) Where biological oxygen demand rises, dissolved oxygen falls, and vice versa: an inverse relationship. *(1 pt)*
(c) Zone B, where DO suddenly falls and BOD jumps just downstream of a sharp change, shows a point-source discharge entering the stream. *(1 pt)*
(d) Dependent variable: number of macroinvertebrate species (species richness). *(1 pt)*
(e) Hypothesis: as dissolved oxygen increases, macroinvertebrate species richness increases (directional or no-relationship statements both testable). *(1 pt)*
(f) Zone A is upstream of the discharge, so it is unaffected by the pollution and gives a baseline for comparison. *(1 pt)*
(g) Cold winter water holds more oxygen (richness could rise) but may fall below some species' tolerance (richness could fall); less sunlight also lowers photosynthesis and DO. Any one linked change earns the point. *(1 pt)*
(h) Raw sewage supplies nutrients and bacteria, so the bacterial population increases. *(1 pt)*
(i) Another abiotic factor: temperature, pH, light, turbidity, salinity or nitrate/phosphate. *(1 pt)*
(j) Persistent organic pollutants bioaccumulate in fatty tissues and biomagnify, reaching the highest concentrations in top consumers and harming them (e.g., neurological toxicity). *(1 pt)*
notes: dup-of-compilation: same item appears in the 2024 FRQ compilation (c20356cb-1751-1796.pdf) which another agent registers. Total 10 points per official guideline for Set 1 Q1 (compilation).

orig_ref: US_24_-_Env_Science_W.pdf, p47-48, FRQ2 (animal protein, GWP and land use)
descriptor: Bar graphs of warming potential and land use per kg of mealworm, chicken, pork and beef protein; survivorship, r-selection, comparing impacts, grazing and sustainable farming.
solution:
(a) Land for 1 kg chicken protein is about 50 m² (read from Figure 2). *(1 pt)*
(b) Darkling beetles, as r-selected species with many offspring and high early mortality, show a Type III survivorship curve. *(1 pt)*
(c) Rapid reproduction and many offspring allow a lot of protein to be produced quickly to meet rising demand. *(1 pt)*
(d) Chicken has lower GWP and lower land use than pork, so it causes less environmental damage (less greenhouse gas or less habitat conversion). *(1 pt)*
(e) Beef has far higher GWP because cattle emit methane, a potent greenhouse gas, and beef needs much more land, which often means forest loss and lost carbon storage. *(1 pt)*
(f) Cattle near streams can erode banks (sediment, turbidity) and deposit manure that adds nutrients and pathogens. *(1 pt)*
(g) Fence the riparian zone, rotate grazing parcels or supply off-stream water. *(1 pt)*
(h) Practices that reduce erosion: no-till or cover crops, contour plowing, terraces, perennial crops. *(1 pt)*
(i) Added advantage, tied to the practice chosen (for example less fuel use and more soil carbon for no-till, farming steeper land for terraces). *(1 pt)*
(j) Climate change may reduce yields through drought, flooding, heat, shifting rainfall and wider pest ranges. *(1 pt)*
notes: dup-of-compilation: same item appears in the 2024 FRQ compilation (c20356cb-1751-1796.pdf) which another agent registers. Graph values read from bars; guideline gives chicken land use as 50 m².

orig_ref: US_24_-_Env_Science_W.pdf, p48-49, FRQ3 (nuclear power, natural gas, trees; calculations)

solution:

orig_ref: US_24_-_Env_Science_W.pdf, p40-41, FRQ1 (succession diagram; forest A versus B clear-cut stream experiment)
descriptor: Primary succession diagram, soil formation, then paired forest watershed experiment with stream stations; identify hypothesis, variables, control, effects of clear-cutting and a golf course.
solution:
(a) Primary succession. *(1 pt)*
(b) Stage II, when lichens, the pioneers, first colonize bare rock. *(1 pt)*
(c) Weathering by wind and rain plus acids from lichens break rock, and dead pioneers add organic matter, forming thin soil. *(1 pt)*
(d) Recreation, aesthetic enjoyment, spiritual use, ecotourism or education. *(1 pt)*
(e) Hypothesis: clear-cutting changes (e.g., raises) stream temperature or other water-quality measures compared with an intact forest. *(1 pt)*
(f) Independent variable: intact versus clear-cut forest (or station location). *(1 pt)*
(g) Forest A is the control for comparison with forest B. *(1 pt)*
(h) Without canopy shade and with added sediment, more sunlight warms the water. *(1 pt)*
(i) Fertilizer runoff adds nitrate and phosphate, causing algal blooms and lower dissolved oxygen (or less turbidity after grass stabilizes soil). *(1 pt)*
(j) Algal decomposition lowers oxygen, killing aquatic organisms; pesticides add toxicity (or less sediment helps gills). *(1 pt)*
notes: dup-of-compilation: same item appears in the 2024 FRQ compilation (c20356cb-1751-1796.pdf) which another agent registers. Total 10 points per guideline for Set 2 Q1.

orig_ref: US_24_-_Env_Science_W.pdf, p42-43, FRQ2 (land use graph; bobcat reintroduction)
descriptor: Stacked graph of habitable land use 1700 to 2018, overgrazing, hypothesis about forest and CO₂, urbanization water problems, bobcats vanishing from farmland and reintroduction.
solution:
(a) 1700 had the highest forest share. *(1 pt)*
(b) From 1700 to 1950 wild grasslands decreased as grazing land increased (inverse relationship). *(1 pt)*
(c) Overgrazing causes loss of vegetation, erosion, compaction or desertification. *(1 pt)*
(d) Refuted: forest share declined, so less photosynthetic carbon uptake and storage, not lower CO₂. *(1 pt)*
(e) Impervious surfaces raise runoff and flooding (or pollution, groundwater overuse, habitat loss). *(1 pt)*
(f) Matching response: permeable pavement, green roofs, retention basins, green space. *(1 pt)*
(g) Forest habitat loss removed food, shelter and mates; hunting or trapping may also have contributed. *(1 pt)*
(h) A small population has low genetic diversity, risks inbreeding and is vulnerable to disease or disturbance. *(1 pt)*
(i) Build habitat corridors linking patches, or restore and reforest habitat. *(1 pt)*
(j) Advantage: corridors help other species and biodiversity, reduce roadkill; restored forest stores carbon and improves water and air. *(1 pt)*
notes: dup-of-compilation: same item appears in the 2024 FRQ compilation (c20356cb-1751-1796.pdf) which another agent registers. Total 10 points per guideline for Set 2 Q2.

orig_ref: INT_24_-_Env_Science_W.pdf, p39-40, FRQ1 (forest ecosystem services; oil-eating bacteria temperature experiment; ocean pH and CO₂)
descriptor: Forest cultural service and water filtration, urbanization effects, oil-degrading bacteria in tanks at three temperatures (dependent variable, hypothesis, replicates, aeration), then pH versus CO₂ graph 1850 to 2100 and coral reefs.
solution:
(a) Cultural service: recreation, aesthetic or spiritual value, ecotourism. *(1 pt)*
(b) Forest roots and soil slow runoff and filter water, trapping sediment and pollutants. *(1 pt)*
(c) Urbanization adds impervious surface, causing runoff, flooding and pollutant loading, which reduces water quality; or it lowers infiltration and groundwater recharge. *(1 pt)*
(d) Dependent variable: crude-oil concentration remaining. *(1 pt)*
(e) Hypothesis: warmer water increases bacterial breakdown, so oil concentration will be lower at higher temperatures. *(1 pt)*
(f) Four replicate tanks per treatment reduce the effect of chance or tank-specific differences and allow averaging. *(1 pt)*
(g) Aerated tanks supply more oxygen to the aerobic bacteria, so oil would break down faster and concentrations would be lower. *(1 pt)*
(h) As CO₂ rises, pH falls: an inverse relationship from 1850 to 2100. *(1 pt)*
(i) CO₂ rise from fossil-fuel burning and deforestation, absorbed by oceans. *(1 pt)*
(j) Supports hypothesis: falling pH lowers carbonate ions, making calcification harder for corals, so reefs would shrink. *(1 pt)*
notes: Points assumed 10 (College Board FRQ standard); no scoring guideline in the Intl file. Not in the 2024 FRQ compilation (different form). Solution written from my own reading; table: 4.5 °C 41 ppm, 12.5 °C 26 ppm, 20.5 °C 9 ppm; 12 tanks.

orig_ref: INT_24_-_Env_Science_W.pdf, p41, FRQ2 (coal power plant diagram; solar; pesticides; fertilizer runoff)
descriptor: Coal-fired plant diagram: smokestack pollutant, reduction method, process at X, coal delivery emissions, solar basics and latitude, then pesticide, IPM and fertilizer runoff solution.
solution:
(a) Pollutants: SO₂, NOx, particulates, mercury or CO. *(1 pt)*
(b) Install scrubbers or use low-sulfur coal to reduce SO₂. *(1 pt)*
(c) At X, steam turns a turbine (water is boiled to steam, or steam condenses). *(1 pt)*
(d) Trains and trucks burn fossil fuels, emitting CO₂. *(1 pt)*
(e) Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly to electricity, or mirrors concentrate heat to make steam. *(1 pt)*
(f) At 60° latitude sunlight strikes at a lower angle and is spread over more area with longer atmospheric path, so output is lower. *(1 pt)*
(g) Pesticides can harm nontarget species or cause resistance. *(1 pt)*
(h) IPM practice: crop rotation, natural predators, resistant varieties or traps. *(1 pt)*
(i) Solution: buffer strips, precise application timing or cover crops. *(1 pt)*
(j) Justify: buffer strips also provide habitat and trap sediment. *(1 pt)*
notes: Points assumed 10. Intl file has only FRQ1 and FRQ2: the file ends at page 41, FRQ3 absent. Part (a)-(c) of 'location X' wording read as stated; X sits at the steam-turbine/condenser stage of the diagram (low confidence).
